title: Episode 20: The Lincoln County War: Billy the Kid and the Merchant Feud
description:
In 1878, Lincoln County, New Mexico exploded into violence when a corrupt merchant and banking monopoly known as 'The House' clashed with an ambitious English rancher named John Tunstall. Following Tunstall's cold-blooded murder, a young ranch hand named William H. Bonney—better known as Billy the Kid—led a vengeful posse of Regulators in a savage war that culminated in a five-day siege in the streets of Lincoln.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. When we think of the Wild West, we often imagine solitary gunfighters dueling at high noon in dusty streets. But the reality was far darker, more organized, and rooted in ruthless corporate greed. In eighteen seventy-eight, Lincoln County, New Mexico—an untamed territory spanning an area larger than Maryland and Massachusetts combined—became the battleground for a vicious commercial monopoly. When an aristocratic young Englishman arrived to challenge the entrenched corrupt establishment, he was assassinated in cold blood. In the bloody retribution that followed, a slight, charismatic nineteen-year-old ranch hand named Billy the Kid would lead a vengeful posse known as the Regulators into a war that consumed an entire territory. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE HOUSE OF DOLAN
In the mid-eighteen seventies, Lincoln County, New Mexico was not merely a county; it was a sprawling frontier empire covering nearly thirty thousand square miles of rugged mountains, desert basins, and pinon-dotted canyons. Every single dollar that flowed through this vast, sun-baked expanse passed through a single, imposing two-story adobe building in the town of Lincoln known simply as 'The House.' Operated by Irish immigrants Lawrence Murphy and James Dolan, The House held an ironclad commercial monopoly over the region. They controlled the only general mercantile store, the only bank, and most critically, lucrative federal military beef contracts with Fort Stanton and the Mescalero Apache reservation. Backed by corrupt territorial politicians and judges in Santa Fe known as the Santa Fe Ring, Murphy and Dolan kept local cattlemen, small homesteaders, and Hispanic farmers trapped in a vicious cycle of perpetual debt and hyper-inflated prices. Anyone who dared to question their authority found their cattle stolen by Dolan's hired rustlers, their mortgages foreclosed by corrupt magistrates, or their lives openly threatened by Dolan-controlled lawmen led by County Sheriff William Brady. Murphy and Dolan ruled Lincoln County like medieval feudal lords, relying on a small army of seasoned gunslingers called the Jesse Evans Gang to enforce their commercial dominance and intimidate anyone who dared to contemplate competition.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE ENGLISH CHALLENGER
The House's comfortable reign ended abruptly in eighteen seventy-six with the arrival of John Henry Tunstall. Tunstall was an ambitious, highly educated twenty-three-year-old English gentleman from a wealthy merchant family, possessing grand dreams of building a massive cattle and banking empire in the American West. Recognizing the immense profits being extracted by Murphy and Dolan, Tunstall partnered with a savvy local attorney named Alexander McSween and legendary cattle baron John Chisum, who grazed more than eighty thousand head of cattle along the Pecos River. Tunstall purchased a vast ranch along the Rio Felix and opened a rival dry goods store and commercial bank directly across the street from The House in Lincoln. Tunstall's new store offered honest prices, low interest rates, and reliable credit, instantly attracting the trade of local ranchers and Hispanic farmers who had felt cheated by Murphy and Dolan for years. Realizing that their commercial monopoly was facing financial ruin, Dolan and Murphy retaliated with fierce legal harassment, filing fraudulent court attachments and sending armed posses to confiscate Tunstall's cattle. But Tunstall refused to back down; instead, he hired a squad of loyal, skilled young ranch hands to protect his livestock and patrol his perimeter. Among these hired ranch hands was an eighteen-year-old orphan and expert marksman who called himself William H. Bonney—a quiet, polite youth who spoke fluent Spanish, loved music, and regarded John Tunstall not merely as an employer, but as the only father figure he had ever known.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: MURDER ON THE TRAIL
The smoldering commercial rivalry turned to outright murder on the freezing morning of February eighteenth, eighteen seventy-eight. Tunstall, accompanied by young Billy Bonney and three other ranch hands, was driving nine prize horses through the snow-dusted pinon hills toward Lincoln. Suddenly, an eighteen-man posse assembled by Sheriff Brady—composed largely of outlaw gunslingers and Dolan partisans—swarmed over the ridge in hot pursuit. As Tunstall's hands scattered into the timber to seek defensive cover, the naive young Englishman rode forward alone, raising his hand peacefully to parley with the approaching riders. Without a single word of warning, Dolan gunfighters William Morton and Jesse Evans leveled their Winchester rifles and shot Tunstall through the chest, knocking him from his saddle, before firing a second bullet into his skull at point-blank range. The murderers then shot Tunstall's horse, laid the dead animal beside the young Englishman, and arranged Tunstall's hat beneath his head in a mocking, grotesque display of frontier cruelty. From the nearby tree line, Billy Bonney watched in helpless horror as his mentor was executed in cold blood and left sprawled face down in the snow, his eyeglasses shattered. Tunstall's murder shattered all illusions of lawful resolution. At Tunstall's funeral in Lincoln, the grief-stricken young Bonney stood over his benefactor's casket and swore a solemn oath: he would not rest until every single man involved in the assassination was dead.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE REGULATORS AND THE BLOOD FEUD
Refusing to accept Sheriff Brady's refusal to arrest the murderers, Alexander McSween obtained legal warrants from the local justice of the peace and formed a special deputized posse named the Regulators. Led by seasoned frontier rancher Dick Brewer and featuring Billy Bonney as its most daring scout, the Regulators rode out across the desert to hunt down Tunstall's killers. The war became relentless, swift, and merciless. In March, the Regulators captured two members of the hit squad, William Morton and Frank Baker, executing them in the Blackwater hills. On the morning of April first, eighteen seventy-eight, Billy and five Regulators concealed themselves behind the corral fence of Tunstall's store, ambushing Sheriff William Brady and his deputy George Hindman as they walked down Lincoln's main street, cutting both men down in a hail of rifle fire. Three days later, at Blazer's Mill in the Mescalero hills, the Regulators cornered a fierce Dolan gunman named Buckshot Roberts. In an epic gun battle inside an adobe cabin, Roberts fought like a wounded lion: despite being mortally wounded in the abdomen, Roberts fatally shot Regulator leader Dick Brewer through the head before succumbing to his wounds. With Brewer dead, the Regulators elected nineteen-year-old Billy Bonney as their field commander, and the conflict escalated from a localized feud into a full-scale territorial civil war that paralyzed southeastern New Mexico.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE FIVE-DAY BATTLE OF LINCOLN
The climax of the Lincoln County War arrived in July eighteen seventy-eight. More than sixty heavily armed men converged on the single dusty street of Lincoln in a catastrophic showdown known as the Five-Day Battle. Billy Bonney and fourteen Regulators barricaded themselves inside Alexander McSween's sprawling twelve-room adobe home, while dozens of Dolan gunmen and newly appointed sheriff George Peppin took up sniper positions in surrounding rooftops and the Wortley Hotel. For four grueling days, the two sides exchanged thousands of rifle rounds under the blazing summer sun, turning the peaceful adobe village into a smoking war zone. The stalemate broke on the fifth day when Colonel Nathan Dudley marched into Lincoln from nearby Fort Stanton with a detachment of United States Army cavalry and a fully loaded twelve-pound Howitzer cannon. Although Dudley claimed official neutrality, his troops aimed their artillery squarely at McSween's house while allowing Dolan's men to approach the building unmolested. At dusk, Dolan snipers crept up and set fire to the wooden roof of McSween's home. As the adobe structure was consumed by roaring flames and choking black smoke, Billy Bonney orchestrated a desperate breakout. With six-guns blazing in both hands, Billy sprinted through the blinding smoke and gunfire, leaping over a stone wall to safety, while Alexander McSween was shot dead in the courtyard.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE LEGEND, LEW WALLACE, AND FORT SUMNER
The dramatic burning of the McSween house ended the war in favor of The House, but it launched Billy the Kid into national frontier folklore. In the autumn of eighteen seventy-eight, President Rutherford B. Hayes removed the corrupt territorial governor and appointed Union Civil War hero General Lew Wallace to restore order. Wallace met secretly with Billy in an adobe cabin in Lincoln, promising him a full executive pardon if he would lay down his arms and testify against Dolan's killers in court. Billy bravely kept his word and testified before the grand jury, but the corrupt Santa Fe district attorney reneged on the agreement, keeping Billy locked in chains. Realizing he had been betrayed by the government, Billy made a spectacular escape, spending the next two years on the run as the most wanted outlaw in America. Meanwhile, Governor Wallace sat in the Palace of the Governors in Santa Fe by candlelight, writing the final chapters of his epic novel Ben-Hur while signing warrants for Billy's capture. Billy's fateful run finally ended at midnight on July fourteenth, eighteen eighty-one, when newly elected Sheriff Pat Garrett slipped into a darkened bedroom at Fort Sumner and shot the twenty-one-year-old outlaw through the heart. Though Billy was dead and buried beneath the dusty soil of Fort Sumner, his defiance against a corrupt corporate monopoly transformed him into an eternal symbol of frontier rebellion.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE VERDICT OF THE FRONTIER
More than a century after Billy the Kid was laid to rest beside his fellow Regulators Tom O'Folliard and Charlie Bowdre at Fort Sumner, the Lincoln County War remains one of the most thoroughly analyzed conflicts in American frontier historiography. Modern legal scholars view the struggle not as a simple morality play of lawful peace officers battling bloodthirsty bandits, but as a violent systemic failure of frontier governance, where entrenched financial cartels captured the mechanisms of municipal law and forced honest citizens into vigilantism. In Lincoln today, the historic adobe courthouse still preserves the bullet hole in the wall where Billy shot Deputy J.W. Bell during his legendary second-story breakout in April eighteen eighty-one. Thousands of visitors travel along Highway three hundred and eighty each year to walk the single quiet street where Tunstall, McSween, and Brady fell. The war demonstrated that when economic monopolists use the legal system as an instrument of extortion, the inevitable consequence is civil catastrophe, forging folk legends from the ashes of forgotten towns.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Lincoln County War was never just a romantic Western shootout; it was a brutal struggle for economic freedom against predatory corporate monopoly in the raw frontier of New Mexico. Through blood, smoke, and betrayal, it forged one of the most enduring legends in American history. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday for the secret city that changed the world. Until then, stay curious.
